question: The assembler's finished work lives in two places: this machine, and the shared copy the other tools read from. Only the shared copy is visible to anyone else. Back in August a run of eighty finished pieces sat on this machine alone for weeks, and you approved sending them up once. That approval covered that one time. I need to know whether sending finished work up is something I just do from now on, or something I ask about each time.

options.name: Send finished work up whenever it is ready
options.what: Anything I finish becomes visible to the other tools the same day. Nothing is ever overwritten or rewritten; work is only ever added on top of what is already there.
options.costs: You lose a look at the work before it becomes visible to the rest of the suite. In practice that look has never caught anything, because the other tools cannot use the work until it is up there anyway.

options.name: Ask you every time
options.what: Nothing becomes visible to the other tools until you say so.
options.costs: Roughly one interruption per finished piece, and any other tool waiting to point at that work waits for you. That is exactly how the eighty piece backlog happened.

recommend.because: The other tools cannot reference our work at all until it is up there, so holding it back does not protect anything, it just delays them. It only ever adds, never replaces, so there is nothing to undo if you dislike something. If you would rather see specific kinds of work first, name the kind and I will hold just those.

detail: Pushing sigil master to origin. Master is currently fully pushed at 8273e5a9, verified by git ls-remote against the remote rather than the local tracking ref. All pushes to date have been fast-forward with no history rewritten. The August incident: origin/master sat at 40f862e2 while local ran 80 commits ahead, making every sigil SHA cited to the aeon lane unfetchable.

question: Forty eight days ago you said the inner workings of the assembler were out of your wheelhouse and told me to make the best decisions and get on with it. Every session since has run on that, and nobody has checked with you once in all that time. It is doing real work, so I am not asking you to withdraw it. I am asking how much you want to hear about what gets decided under it.

options.name: Keep it as it is, and hear about it at milestones
options.what: I keep deciding, and you get told when a whole piece of work finishes rather than when each call inside it gets made.
options.costs: You will occasionally find out about a design choice after it is already built into everything. Unwinding one at that point is a day or two rather than a conversation.

options.name: Keep it, but tell you the notable calls as they happen
options.what: Same authority, but the handful of choices per piece of work that a person could reasonably disagree with get written down for you as they are made.
options.costs: A few short notes per piece of work landing on your screen. You can ignore them and lose nothing, but they are still there to read.

options.name: Take it back and decide these yourself
options.what: Internal choices come to you before they are built.
options.costs: Several decisions a day, most of them about things you told me you had no interest in. Work stops between each one.

recommend.because: Keeping the authority is clearly right, since it has produced a working assembler without you having to think about any of it. The only thing worth changing is that right now nothing is written down for you at all, so the first you hear of a choice is when something built on it goes wrong. A short note per notable call costs me nothing and gives you a place to object early.

detail: The banked directive lives in this lane's session memory as user-defers-sigil-technical-calls, written ~2026-07-05, origin session 9ff8029c, recording the owner's own words: the internals are 'out of my wheelhouse', 'make the best decisions'. git log -S confirms it has never appeared in any sigil doc, so until 2026-08-22 every cold boot took the whole posture from an unauditable memory file. Empyrean reports the owner confirmed it directly to them on 2026-08-23; held here as their report rather than as an answer, since a relay retires the check rather than performing it.

question: The tool I look after is two things at once. It is a machine that turns the game's source into a cartridge, and it is also the language that source is written in. You told me the machine half is mine to decide. The language half is different: adding a new word to it changes what every future page of game source looks like, and it is close to impossible to take one back once the game is written using it. I have been treating any new word as yours and everything else as mine, and I want to know if that is where you want the line drawn. This is the one of my three questions that is actually holding work up.

options.name: Any new word in the language comes to you
options.what: I decide how the machine works and how anything already in the language is spelled. Anything genuinely new waits for you.
options.costs: Two warnings the build has been printing since the eighteenth of August cannot be cleared, because clearing them needs a new way of writing one kind of import. They will keep printing until you rule. Every future addition waits on you the same way.

options.name: New words are mine unless they change what ends up on the cartridge
options.what: I can add ways of writing things that produce exactly the same cartridge bytes as today. Anything that changes what actually gets written into the cartridge still comes to you.
options.costs: The language grows without your sign off. The risk is a word you would not have chosen becoming normal across the game source before you see it. It is bounded by the fact that none of it can change the game as it runs.

options.name: The language is mine too, and you see it at milestones
options.what: I decide the whole thing and report at the end of each piece of work.
options.costs: You would be finding out about the shape of the language the game is written in after it is already written that way. This is the hardest one to reverse.

recommend.because: It splits on the thing that actually matters to you. A new way of writing something that produces an identical cartridge is a matter of taste in the source, and you have already said the source machinery is mine. A construct that changes what the cartridge contains is a real design decision about the game and should be yours. It clears the two stuck warnings immediately, and the padding construct that is genuinely a design call stays with you, which is where I think you want it.

detail: Concretely: the closure-edge import spelling that kills the two CORPUS_OPEN_FINDINGS rows (import.no-names, first_observed 2026-08-18, in crates/sigil-cli/tests/warn_tier_corpus.rs) is byte-neutral by construction and would fall to me under emit_line. pad_to(N) moves bytes the author did not write and stays with the owner under either as_now or emit_line. The current docs/OVERSEER.md scope line reads as as_now. Spec 2 4.3 already forbids compiler-inserted padding outright, which is why pad_to(N) needed empyrean's ruling and spec text rather than an implementation.
